item.title: The Disorderly Transition to Multipolarity
item.description: Prof. Glenn Diesen
item.dc:creator: Glenn Diesen
item.content:encoded:
The international system naturally gravitates toward an international balance of power, in which no one state or group of states can dictate to the rest. The balance of power, which constrains all the major powers, can be disrupted if a great power is defeated at war or collapses from within. Yet, states do not balance themselves and will pursue expansionist policies when unconstrained. The predictable consequence is thus that the unbalanced power will pursue expansionist policies that exhaust it, while other rising powers at the periphery will begin to collectively balance the hegemon. The international system would thus gravitate back toward an equilibrium.

The Brief Unipolar Moment

The collapse of the Soviet Union disrupted the international balance of power, as the world was left with only one superpower. The consequence was predictable: the U.S. would embrace a hegemonic security strategy that would make peace dependent on global primacy. Without any checks on its power, the U.S. would expand in every direction in terms of engaging in wars and expanding military alliances such as NATO. Strategic thinking deteriorates as the hegemon can be everywhere and does not need to prioritize, while it can also make many mistakes as it can absorb the costs of its follies.

However, the U.S. would eventually exhaust itself with unsustainable debt, and at home the empire would create economic inequalities, social problems, democratic deficits, and political instability. As the hegemon must prevent the rise of rivals to maintain a unipolar distribution of power, rising powers such as China, Russia, India, and others collectively balance the U.S. New political organizations like BRICS and the SCO emerge, new security arrangements emerge, and there is growing economic cooperation in technology, industry, transportation corridors, banks, payment systems, trade in national currencies, etc.

A Failed Strategy for Restoring Global Primacy

The U.S. has the option of either adjusting to the new multipolar distribution of power or attempting to restore global hegemony. The U.S. decided on the latter and has recognized that the former format for global primacy is no longer sustainable. The U.S. must weaken its strategic rivals, which has taken the form of an economic war against China, a proxy war using Ukrainians to fight and weaken Russia, and a regime-change war against Iran. All of these wars are failing and have only intensified the shift to a multipolar system by decoupling economically from the U.S. and collectively balancing against the U.S.

Furthermore, the legitimacy of “liberal hegemony” is collapsing. The premise that U.S. global primacy elevated liberal democratic values and stability is being undermined by lawless forever wars, genocide, regime changes, the kidnapping of state leaders, threats of eliminating entire civilizations, the stealing of sovereign funds, restrictions on freedom of navigation, endless sanctions, etc.

The U.S. must also change its relationship with its allies, as it is overextended and must cut costs and increase the return on the investment put into its empire. Restoring primacy means that frontline states must give privileged market access to the U.S. and sever their ties with China, Russia, etc. Frontline states must also shift their production and investments to the U.S., and states like Denmark should cede strategic territory. The frontline states must also pay more for their own security and use this military power to fight and weaken strategic rivals such as China, Russia, and Iran.

The weakness of the strategy is its unattainable objective. Frontline states are asked to sacrifice their national interests for the U.S., while the U.S. has a diminishing capacity to enhance their economies or security. As the Gulf States and Europeans are discovering, the U.S. alliance system invites wars rather than preventing them. This problem is also being discussed now in East Asia.

The Europeans are especially compliant, as their entire security architecture and economic model depend on the U.S. However, even the submissive Europeans must eventually adjust to new realities by diversifying their economic connectivity, reducing their warmongering posture, and shifting their focus to national interests. Failure to do so by the current political leaders creates a political legitimacy problem that will give rise to new and untested political forces that will make the required changes.

The U.S. will see its strategic rivals finding common cause in collectively balancing against the U.S., while its weakened frontline states are destabilized. With the growing costs of pursuing unipolar policies in a multipolar world, new political forces will also emerge in the U.S. that will pursue national interests by adjusting to the international distribution of power.

Toward a New Equilibrium

It is not easy for the U.S. or its allies to accept the transition from a unipolar to a multipolar world. The current political class, raised over the past 3.5 decades, was told they presided over the “end of history” and ushered in the era of perpetual peace. Fueled by ideology, they believed the Political West would dominate in perpetuity to the benefit of all mankind. That ideological fantasy lives on long after the distribution of power has changed.

The U.S. will eventually scale back its empire so the other great powers will balance each other instead of the U.S., allowing the U.S. to retreat and recover its strength. The coming economic crisis will make the situation dire, and the option now is either an organized retrenchment or a disorganized retreat. The world will naturally gravitate toward a new equilibrium and, hopefully, not destroy itself during the disorderly transition.

item.title: Ratcliffe’s Moscow Trip: A Visit Before the Storm
item.description: Prof. Glenn Diesen
item.dc:creator: Glenn Diesen
item.content:encoded:
There will unavoidably be a lot of speculation about CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s brief visit to Moscow due to the secrecy surrounding it, and media stories must conform to the war narratives. We are told that this was a routine visit and nothing out of the ordinary, although in reality, this was the first visit by a CIA director since November 2021. Given the deteriorating situation between NATO and Russia, we can draw some conclusions about the likely purpose of the visit.

The visit was likely intended to deliver a message and a threat to Moscow as desperation grows in Washington. NATO and Russia are now in the most dangerous period ever in their history of conflict. The CIA has been in charge of the Ukraine proxy war against Russia since the coup in 2014, and massive escalations can be expected as it all falls apart.

The Ukraine Proxy War is Unravelling

The Ukrainian army is exhausted and collapsing across the frontlines; the economy is falling apart due to the naval blockade and destruction of critical infrastructure; there is growing social upheaval from the aggressive “recruitment” of military conscripts and economic problems; the political crisis could bring down the government; NATO is running out of money and weapons to keep the proxy war going; and political opposition is growing across Europe that cannot be suppressed forever.

The US is bogged down in Iran and facing an economic crisis, while Russia is assisting Iran and has become the leading partner of China in establishing an alternative international economic architecture. The US wars against Russia and Iran, as well as the economic war against China, were intended to knock out or roll back the key adversaries on the Eurasian continent to restore US global primacy. Instead, these wars have intensified the shift toward a multipolar world order, as the US is facing defeat on all fronts and has exhausted itself militarily and economically, while the stability of the US political system is going from bad to worse. The US has pushed its main Eurasian adversaries together in what can only be described as Kissinger’s worst nightmare, and the Political West is fragmenting from imperial overstretch and the absence of a post-hegemonic economic model.

Trump continues to insist that the US has defeated Iran and the Strait of Hormuz is open and under US control, while NATO continues to insist that “Ukraine is winning”. As NATO’s proxy war in Ukraine begins to falter, NATO will likely escalate, as seen by Britain’s reckless actions. Russia, on its part, will likely escalate against Ukraine toward a knockout blow and take a tougher line with NATO to restore its deterrence, as NATO crossed the boundaries between proxy war and direct war long ago. Deterring NATO does not entail an invasion, but imposing a cost in the form of covert operations or even direct strikes are options for enforcing Russia’s red lines. Although, at the moment, the priority is to put an end to the proxy war without unnecessary escalation with NATO.

Reviving Diplomacy?

So what was Ratcliffe doing in Moscow? How can the US use diplomacy to improve its situation? It seems highly unlikely that NATO is prepared to give up its large Ukrainian proxy army by agreeing to any peace agreement that would restore Ukraine’s neutrality and resolve the territorial dispute. Much like the war with Iran, diplomatic initiatives are intended to secure a pause to regroup and shape the battlefield more favorably.

The 40+ day campaign by Ukraine and NATO to strike civilian infrastructure deep inside Russia did not break Russia, rather it backfired in a big way. Ratcliffe likely wanted an end to the naval blockade by returning to the rules of the grain deal, a ceasefire against energy infrastructure, and a halt to the offensive against the cities of Slovyansk, Kramatorsk, and Zaporizhzhia. There are likely also concerns in Washington about Russia preparing to open up yet another front in the Chernigov region. Such initiatives are, much like the EU-proposed unconditional ceasefire, intended to prolong the war rather than put an end to it.

It therefore also seems highly unlikely that Russia will make any concessions, as Russia cannot make any significant concessions. If this was a war about territorial expansion, then NATO escalation and pressure may have produced some Russian concessions. However, the uncomfortable truth that the political-media establishment in NATO refuses to accept is that Russia considers NATO’s incursion into Ukraine to be an existential threat. Whether or not NATO agrees with this assessment is completely irrelevant as Russia will act on its conviction. This suggests Russia has very little room for concessions.

The conflict could have been resolved at any time since 2014 by ending NATO expansion and restoring Ukraine’s neutrality. In the absence of any political settlement that ensures this objective, Russia will strip Ukraine of the high-value territory that can be used as a NATO frontline against Russia, and the rest of Ukraine will be reduced to a dysfunctional landlocked rump state. This solution will create a terribly difficult future for Ukraine and decades of instability for both NATO and Russia, yet from Moscow’s perspective it is the only possible path as NATO will not stop expanding and restoring Ukraine’s neutrality.

The optimist in me would like to think that Ratcliffe’s visit was intended to strengthen diplomatic channels and coordination to navigate through the extremely dangerous time we are heading into. Although, it seems more likely that diplomacy still takes the form of more ultimatums and threats in the hope of rescuing the situation. Predictably, this will not be received well in Moscow where the anger is boiling over

.
